title: The Potomac River Midair Collision
content:
How America’s Golden Age of Aviation Safety Came To an End

It was a clear and mild evening in America’s capital, warm enough to melt the concreted banks of nearly month-old snow and send the last frigid fragments of ice fleeing down the dark waters of the Potomac. Above the black expanse of the river, aircraft approaching Washington National Airport were strung across the sky like a chain of Christmas lights, lining up for the last big push before traffic trailed off into the night. The clock read 8:47 p.m.

By January 2025, it had been nearly 16 years since the last time a major disaster befell a US airline. Countless aviation professionals had begun, developed, and even ended their careers without ever seeing one. On an intellectual level, all understood the statistical certainty that that record would one day end, and that the time and place of its ending, whether it be today or 10 years from now, in New York or Alaska, could not be predicted. And when it finally did happen, at 8:47 p.m. on the 29th of January 2025, at a height of 278 feet above the Potomac River in Washington D.C., it was difficult to comprehend that that day had in fact been today, and that an unprecedented period of safety had suddenly been consigned to the past. But for many who flew or worked in that hectic, benighted airspace, the fact that it ended at National Airport was not a surprise: their sentiment tinged by hindsight, they collectively said, “If it had to be anywhere, it would have been DCA.”

How could it be that such a tragedy retroactively struck so many as inevitable? The fact is that some people did see it, or something like it, coming from a long way off. And the story of how it was nevertheless allowed to happen is one that spans decades, disciplines, and institutions, from the cockpits of the two downed aircraft to the halls of Congress itself. It was born out of a web of interlocking interests and policies that formed a seemingly intractable milieu of dysfunction, in which those who had the whole picture lacked the power to change it, and those who did have the power to effect change did not see the whole picture.

Now, lubricated by the shock of disaster, the gears of bureaucracy have begun to turn, advancing safety improvements that will help make American airspace safer. But even as I write this, the same forces that created the conditions for that disaster remain at work, steadily pushing us into the jaws of the next one.

Chapter 1: The Last Ten Minutes

The flight from Wichita to Washington had been uneventful thus far for 34-year-old Captain Jonathan Campos and his first officer, 28-year-old Sam Lilley. The route was a relatively new one, inaugurated just a year earlier at the behest of Senator Jerry Moran and local officials in Wichita, who wanted to connect Washington, D.C. to the most populous city in Kansas, the city that billed itself as “The Air Capital of the World,” home to Cessna, Beechcraft, and Spirit Aerosystems.[2] The crew had begun their day there, at Wichita’s Dwight D. Eisenhower National Airport, fresh off a 20-hour rest break between the second and third days of a four-day trip sequence that had already taken them to Charlotte, North Carolina and Lafayette, Louisiana.[1:10] Such was the life of a regional airline pilot in America — hotels in second and third tier cities, fast food at small airports, cramped jets with two-by-two seating.

Captain Campos had worked since 2019 for PSA Airlines, a wholly-owned regional subsidiary of American Airlines, where he had begun his airline career on the Canadair Regional Jet, or CRJ, a twin rear-engine jet designed and built in Canada by Bombardier, both independently and later under contract for Mitsubishi. PSA operates a single-type fleet of 140 CRJs, consisting of both 65-passenger CRJ-700s and 76-passenger CRJ-900s, all of which bear American Airlines livery and fly under the brand name American Eagle. Most passengers probably pay no attention to the fine print on both their tickets and the aircraft itself, which is required by law to state “Operated by PSA Airlines.”

In more than five years with PSA, about half of them as captain, Campos had accumulated just shy of 4,000 flying hours, with three quarters of them on the CRJ series. First Officer Lilley had joined the company later, in 2022, and had just short of 2,500 hours, with 965 on the type. Both pilots were still near the beginning of their respective careers, and both were known for their passion, skill, and professionalism,[1:9–11] all hallmarks of a pair who were likely to keep climbing up the ladder into the major airlines, the common aspiration of most young aviators starting out at what they call “the regionals.”

Neither pilot would have perceived anything unusual about the evening flight to Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport on January 29, 2025. Captain Campos had flown there 39 times before; Lilley, 43 times.[1:10–11] They would have known the common approaches by name, recognized the navigational landmarks, and understood the airport’s frenetic pace of operations.

◊◊◊

Descending through the mid-level airspace around Washington, the Potomac TRACON slotted them into the queue for the active approach to National Airport, the Mount Vernon visual approach to runway 1, proceeding up the Potomac River from the south. The TRACON swung them far to the south over Virginia, then turned them back around for a long, straight final, handing them over to the Washington tower at 20:43 local time.

Though night had long since fallen over the nation’s capital, visibility was almost unlimited, and the pilots would have seen a long chain of airplanes stretching out ahead of them, descending on an invisible three-degree slope toward the distant lights of the runway. Over the pilots’ headsets, the tower frequency hummed with activity as the Local controller brought them in, landing an aircraft every minute, with departures squeezed in between.

Using their PSA callsign and flight number, First Officer Lilley opened communication with a routine position report. “Tower, Bluestreak 5342 on Mount Vernon visual runway one.”

“Bluestreak 5342, Washington tower, winds are three two zero at one seven, gusts two five,” the controller replied. “Can you take runway three three?”[1:361]

Although most aircraft land on National Airport’s primary runway, designated 1 or 19 depending on the direction of use, the field has two other shorter runways, designated 15/33 and 4/22, respectively, which cross both runway 1/19 and each other to form a rough triangle. These auxiliary runways are too short to regularly accommodate larger airplanes, but PSA’s smaller CRJs could usually handle them, and Campos and Lilley were well aware that Washington tower liked to divert these regional jets to 15/33 when traffic was heavy in order to free up space on 1/19. At many regional airlines operating into National Airport, it had become standard practice to calculate performance figures for landing on runway 15/33 ahead of time, even if initially cleared to land on 1/19, so that the pilots could quickly accept or decline an offer to switch.[4–3:10:00–3:14:00]

The pilot has final authority over whether to accept an offer to land on runway 15/33, even if they know the airplane is capable of doing so. Some pilots preferred not to land on that runway if they could help it, including the PSA flight in line ahead of flight 5342, whose curt reply to an identical offer, “unable tonight,” was captured on the air traffic control tower tapes.[1:360] But most were aware that accepting the approach made the controllers’ lives easier.

Upon hearing the request, Captain Campos simply asked, “Do we got the numbers for it,” referring to the landing performance figures.

Having already performed the calculations ahead of time, First officer Lilley replied, “Yeah, I think so,” then, perhaps double checking his work, added, “Yeah, it’s uh, it’s the same numbers.”[1:361]

Campos was reluctant to accept. Runway 33 would impose a higher workload because it was a circling approach, requiring them to break off the glide path to runway 1, disconnect the autopilot and begin manual flight, circle with reference to landmarks, and align visually with the runway just before touchdown, all while maintaining the approach reference speed and the optimal glide path, listening to air traffic control communications, and watching for traffic.[1:152–153] It probably wasn’t the way Campos wanted to spend the last ten minutes of the flight, especially when he could just say “unable,” carry on straight ahead, and land. But he had the numbers, and he was a conscientious man. “I really don’t want to, but I guess uhhh tell ‘em…” he started to say.

“I mean, I can just tell ‘em — ” Lilley interrupted, offering to turn down the request, just as their colleagues had.

But Campos had made up his mind. “Nah, it’s fine, we got the numbers for it,” he said. “Yeah tell ’em we’re fine. We’ll do three three, we’ll do it.”

Lilley hopped on the radio and transmitted, “Yeah, we can do uh, three three for Bluestreak 5342.”

“Bluestreak 5342, at the Wilson Bridge change to cir — change to circle runway three three,” the controller replied. “Runway three three cleared to land.”

Lilley read back the clearance, and then Campos launched into the required approach briefing. “Three three,” he began. “Thousand feet at the uh, highway, five hundred over the church.”[1:362–363]

Because the circling approach to 33 was to be conducted visually, it was flown with reference to landmarks only, and since no official procedure for this approach had been published by the Federal Aviation Administration, airlines had devised their own in accordance with FAA guidelines. The procedure used by PSA was to break off the runway 1 approach path at the Woodrow Wilson Bridge on Interstate 95, then follow Interstate 295 — “the highway” — to the northeast while descending through 1,000 feet, followed by a left turn to align with the runway, passing overhead Bolling Chapel — “the church” — on Joint Base Anacostia-Bolling at 500 feet.[1:157] From there, landing should be straightforward, and other than these two points there was little for the pilots to brief.

First Officer Lilley acknowledged Campos’s approach brief, and Campos added, “I’ll just disconnect everything and we’ll go from there,” indicating his intention to disengage the autopilot at the Wilson Bridge, which was standard practice.

As cross-talk between the controller and various other aircraft continued in the background, the pilots completed the landing checklist, extending the flaps to 30 degrees and selecting gear down. The familiar rumble of the landing gear deployment filled the cockpit for several seconds, then the pilots verified that the gear was down, set flaps 45, and confirmed that the flight spoilers were stowed.

“Before landing checklist complete,” Lilley declared.[1:364–366]

Outside, the immense bulk of the tidewater Potomac stretched out to their left and right, its banks lined with upscale, wooded neighborhoods, their streetlights piercing the dark to form neat little constellations. Ahead, the lights of cars streamed across the Wilson Bridge and past the MGM Hotel & Casino at National Harbor.

At 20:45, flight 5342 overflew the bridge, and Captain Campos declared, “Visual three three.” He disengaged the autopilot, triggering the autopilot disconnect warning, which silenced itself after a few seconds.

Taking full manual control, Campos steered to the right, breaking away from the orderly queue headed for runway 1 to line up on interstate 295 instead. Lilley confirmed all checks were complete, and Campos confirmed that they were configured to land. Everything had been done by the book.[1:368–369]

Transmissions to other aircraft continued to play over the speakers, a steady staccato of traffic pouring into, out of, and through the tightly controlled airspace around National Airport.

“Jazz 789, contact Potomac Departure, good day.”*

*Bizarre fact: This Jazz aircraft was the same one that was later destroyed in the March 2026 runway collision at LaGuardia.

“American 3130, slow to final.”

“Slowin’, American 3130.”

“PAT 25, traffic just south of Wilson Bridge is a CRJ at one thousand two hundred feet, circling to runway three three.”

There was no indication that either pilot noticed that this transmission was referring to them. Somewhere out in that dense mess of lights, a helicopter was being told to keep them in sight.

“Uhhh I gotta level off,” Campos said, watching their altitude.

“Vis separation approved,” the tower said to the unseen, unheard helicopter.

“American 1630, tower, runway one line up and wait, traffic is three out, circling runway three three, additional traffic on a six mile final.”

“Alright,” Lilley said, in response to Campos’s comment.[1:369–370]

The crosstalk continued, turning into a constant background drone.

“Line up and wait runway one, American 1630.”

“American 72 by KATRN, runway one.”

“MUSL 7, standby.”

“Bluestreak 5307, keep rolling out to November, ground point seven, good day.”

In the cockpit, the ground proximity warning system called out “one thousand,” and Lilley repeated, “thousand feet.”

“Stable, spoilers stowed, confirm missed approach altitude set,” Campos said, running through the same lines he had said a thousand times before.

“Uh, two thousand two hundred set,” said Lilley.

“November, 5307,” an aircraft acknowledged over the tower frequency.[1:371]

“American 1630, winds are at three two zero at one four gusting two five, traffic is a two mile left base runway three three, no delay, runway one clear for immediate takeoff.”

“Number one, cleared for takeoff, American 1630,” the American Airlines pilot replied.[1:372]

On board flight 5342, the pilots were likely watching flight 1630, monitoring its departure from runway 1 to ensure it passed the intersection with runway 33 before they got too close to touchdown.

“MUSL 7 say request?”

“MUSL 7 did you say route three to zone six?”

“MUSL 7 approved.”

“American 472, Mount Vernon visual one,” said yet another aircraft.[1:373]

“Medevac Air Care one, Washington Tower, National altimeter two niner niner zero, approved through Washington class bravo airspace, report landing assured at Fairfax.”

In the cockpit, the automated voice called out, “five hundred.” Just below and to their left, street lighting illuminated the steeple of the Bolling Chapel. “Five hundred feet, on top of the bug, sinking seven, stable,” Lilley called out, reporting that they were on speed and descending at the expected rate.

“Checks,” Campos acknowledged.

“I got two white, two red,” Lilley added, referring to the four lights of the precision approach path indicator next to the runway, which showed them on the optimal glide path.

“Cool,” said Campos.[1:374]

Over the radio another message came through, its significance possibly escaping the busy PSA pilots. “PAT 25, you got that CRJ in sight?” In the background, a faint beeping sound could be heard, which the pilots would not have known was the sound of a conflict alert at the controller’s work station.

At almost the same time, the CRJ’s traffic collision avoidance system called out, “Traffic, traffic.” Neither pilot acknowledged, but ahead of them they could see American 1630 crossing runway 33 and climbing away into the darkness. As it departed, the callouts ceased.

“PAT 25, pass behind the CRJ,” the controller said to the unseen helicopter, his voice still backed by the incessant beeping of the conflict alert. The pilots of flight 5342 would not have heard the helicopter’s reply, but they would have trusted that the tower was taking care of it.

“Vis separation,” the controller said again to the helicopter.[1:375]

The inbound aircraft that had just called was calling again. “American 472 at BADDN, Mount Vernon visual.”

On flight 5342, the ground proximity warning system called out that they were 100 feet above minimums. With the runway in sight, the callout was immaterial, and Captain Campos continued his left turn to align with runway 33.

“American 47 — ” the controller started to say.

Suddenly, something large and fast surged into the pilots’ peripheral vision, just below them and to the right. Perhaps they had time to see that it was a US Army Sikorsky UH-60 Blackhawk helicopter, its blades slicing a path through the dark toward their plane, or maybe all they ever saw was a flash of movement and a streak of light.

Either way, at the last possible second Captain Campos hauled his controls all the way back, his sharp maneuver punctuated by an exclamation of surprise, followed by a shout of terror from his first officer.[1:9, 376] But it was too late.

Flight 5342 was still in a left bank, its nose rising through 7 degrees, when the helicopter’s furious rotor slashed into the underside of the aft fuselage and left wing. In an instant, pieces of rotor blades ripped through the CRJ’s left main landing gear, fuselage skin, wing-to-body fairing, and left wing forward spar, dealing catastrophic structural damage to both aircraft.[1:95–98] An explosion lit up the night as liberated fuel ignited, and the CRJ’s left wing split in two, sending the aircraft rolling into a left-hand spiral from which there would be no escape. Just 4.7 seconds later, flight 5342 plunged into the freezing waters of the Potomac River, followed almost simultaneously by the remains of the hapless helicopter, whose three crewmembers never knew what hit them.

◊◊◊

In the tower, the controller’s transmission continued briefly: “…2, Washington Tower, winds are three two zero at one seven,” but in the background, audible shouting could be heard, and he trailed off, catching sight of the unfolding catastrophe.

For a moment, there was silence, and then American 472 said, “Oh, they just went — “

“Tower, did you see that!?” American 3130 asked.

Doing his best to remain professional, but with an edge creeping into his voice, the controller said, “American 472 — American 3130, go around, turn left heading three five zero, climb and maintain three thousand!”[6–02:32]

One by one, the controller diverted each flight from its approach, clearing the way for rescue vehicles to pour onto the runway in response to the frantically ringing crash bell. He carried on because he had to; it was his job. Minutes later, he was relieved from his post, and the investigation began.

Out at the banks of the river, every manner of first responder rushed toward the scene, their floodlights illuminating the shattered, upturned hull of the CRJ, its wreckage resting in water just a few feet deep. Boats launched within minutes, plowing through floating ice and debris to reach the wreckage, but what they found there left them bereft of hope. Soon they were hauling bodies back to shore, and even as news channels around the country and indeed the world broke into their programming to report on the apparent disaster, those who bravely deployed to the scene had already come to the grim conclusion that there were no survivors.

◊◊◊

Aboard flight 5342, there had been 60 passengers and 4 crewmembers, who came from all walks of life, but some walks were more represented than others. A few were solo business travelers; there was a group of friends coming home from a hunting vacation; but nearly half, 28 in total, were affiliated with the U.S. Figure Skating team’s national development camp for promising youth skaters, held in Wichita in the days before the accident. Among them were 11 young figure skaters from the northeast, all aged 11 to 16, some of whom might one day have represented America at the Olympics, if not for a sudden and terrible twist of fate. Many of their parents perished alongside them, whole families vanishing into the Potomac. Coaches and staff were lost too, including Evgenia Shishkova and Vadim Naumov, a Russian skating couple who had won the pairs title at the 1994 World Championships, and had since come to the United States to teach a new generation of athletes.[7] Their absence would be felt around the world.

In all, 67 lives were lost, including two pilots and two flight attendants on the CRJ and three servicemembers on the Blackhawk. It was the first major air disaster involving a US airline since 2009, the deadliest since 2001, and the first airliner to be lost in a mid-air collision in US airspace since 1986, reviving a threat that had once been consigned to history. Coming just nine days into a new presidential administration, the aura of crisis was palpable, and accusations of blame flew within hours. Most were utterly unfounded. Others asked pressing questions: had the amount of traffic into National Airport exceeded the capacity of the air traffic controllers? What was being done to keep helicopters and airliners apart?

With the benefit of hindsight, now that the investigation is complete and the facts have been laid on the table, what happened on the night of January 29, 2025 might best be described using the framework outlined by Charles Perrow in his landmark 1984 book, Normal Accidents.

A “normal accident” is an emergent disaster, arising from a complex and highly technical system whose components are tightly coupled, meaning that the state of one component significantly affects others. Perrow wrote that in simple mechanical systems, a high degree of reliability can be achieved through the use of independent and redundant components, but as system complexity increases, especially when human organizations are involved, true redundancy among the components ceases to exist, and failures or errors may trigger a “cascade” that propagates through the system until disaster occurs.[8] Cascades are, by their very nature, difficult or impossible to fully predict until they occur. In this sense, the midair collision over the Potomac River may not qualify, because it was in fact predicted. But by the time those predictions were made, the vulnerabilities in the tightly coupled air traffic system already existed and the cascade needed only to be set in motion; the failure to act on knowledge of its existence simply became another cataract.

[Read profiles of all 67 lives lost]

Sometimes, when I write about air disasters, I use the term “sequence of events,” and the article forms a chronological narrative. In reality, however, there’s rarely such a thing as a sequence of events, with a single origin point and a perceptible chain of dominoes leading to the self-evident endpoint. In fact, there’s no such thing as an origin point at all; we perceive the existence of such points only because thinking in other terms is impractical. Instead, when telling the story of flight 5342, I want to strike a middle ground by imagining the existence of an event web, in which multiple concurrently existing strands became woven together across time and space, coupling the components of the complex system in such a way that Perrow’s cascade became not only possible, but inevitable.

The boundaries of the event web are indefinite and subjective, defined only by the scope we set for ourselves. The scope of each National Transportation Safety Board investigation is defined by law; the scope I have chosen is somewhat wider, because the NTSB is limited to analysis of the aviation system, while I think this accident cannot be fully understood unless outside pressures on that system are also considered. Either way, held back by the human need for linear storytelling, I’ve broken down that web into several major component strands, each of which has been given its own dedicated chapter. None of those strands are independent and their separation into several storylines is purely artificial, but like unfolding a tesseract into three dimensions, it’s one way to transform the event web into something we feeble human beings can wrap our minds around.

What follows is the full story of the Potomac River midair collision.

◊◊◊

Chapter 2: America’s (Least?) Favorite Airport

Anyone who flies to National Airport can hardly help but marvel at its location. Jammed up against the very heart of Washington, the threshold of runway 19 is only four kilometers from the White House and the Capitol Building, and runway 33 is aimed directly at the Pentagon, whose southeast wall looms just 1,400 meters from the end of the asphalt. However, having admired these national landmarks, the next things a traveler will notice are the large crowds and long wait times at the gates, baggage claim, and security. These two sets of observations are in fact linked, not only to each other, but perhaps to the accident as well.

The fact that DCA is notoriously busy is well known inside and outside of the aviation industry, and the fact that a midair collision took place at an airport widely seen as overcrowded struck most observers as unlikely to be coincidental. In the early days and weeks after the disaster, it was practically taken as gospel that excessive traffic at DCA had increased the background risk levels by eroding separation margins between aircraft and placing excessive workloads on air traffic controllers. But I don’t take anything as gospel. Before we get into the nitty-gritty of what happened on the day of the accident, I want to take the time to establish what the background risk level at DCA actually was, including whether the level of traffic was actually excessive. The purpose of this Chapter is to lay that groundwork by answering three questions: what were the traffic levels at DCA; were those levels excessive; and if so, why?

◊◊◊

National Airport, or DCA, was built in 1941 as the primary commercial airport for Washington, D.C., but it was never meant to retain that status for very long. Hemmed in on three sides by the Potomac River and by the George Washington Memorial Parkway on the fourth, the airport never had much room to expand, and the layout of its three runways, with each crossing both of the others, limited their usefulness in accommodating additional traffic. As early as 1950, lawmakers directed the construction of what would become Dulles International Airport in northern Virginia in order to serve both long-haul international flights and additional domestic flights that could not be accommodated by DCA, which was already nearing its design capacity. However, as anyone from the area knows, this is not exactly what happened. In fact, even today DCA serves 86% as many passengers per year as Dulles does — 24.9 million versus 29 million as of 2025 — in a facility with less than 7% of Dulles’s land area.[9][10][11][12]

Part of the problem is that DCA is so conveniently located, just a few minutes by train or taxi from downtown Washington, Arlington, and Alexandria; in fact, if you’re among the many thousands who live in Crystal City or Aurora Highlands, the airport can be quickly and conveniently accessed on foot, no transportation needed. This makes DCA one of several airports in America where demand substantially outstrips capacity, necessitating a federal slot control program to limit the number of flights that may operate there.

In theory, a slot control program is established by the Federal Aviation Administration and implemented through the FAA’s Slot Office.[13][4–3:17:25] If you, like me, are masochistic enough to regularly find yourself reading the Code of Federal Regulations, you may eventually discover that in CFR Title 14, Chapter I, Subchapter F, Part 93, Subpart K, there is a list of slot-controlled airports consisting of LaGuardia, John F. Kennedy International, and Washington National,* with a set of tables listing how many air carrier, commuter, and general aviation or air taxi operations under instrument flight rules are permitted per specified time period, unless otherwise authorized by air traffic control.

*The cited CFR says that O’Hare and Newark are also slot controlled, but this is no longer true.

In the interest of clarity, for our purposes a flight under “instrument flight rules” means operating under a filed flight plan with respect to published navigational information and subject to air traffic control. That’s essentially every aircraft that ever lands at any of these airports, so we don’t need to worry about that too much just yet.

A slot, in the simplest terms, is permission for either one takeoff or one landing by an aircraft operated by a specified company during a specific time period — a calendar hour, in the case of DCA. The Department of Transportation awards the slots to different air carriers through something that resembles, but technically is not, a bidding process.[14] The number of hourly slots set by the FAA for DCA has been retained since 1987 at 37 for mainline air carriers, 11 for commuter airlines, and 12 for general aviation and air taxis, for a total of 60.[13][14] However, the reality of DCA operations is quite different, almost entirely due to interference by the United States Congress.

It is common knowledge in both aviation and politics that DCA is the preferred airport for Senators and Representatives who must regularly travel between their home states or districts and the United States Capitol. The reasons for their preference are largely the same as everyone else’s. However, unlike the rest of us, they are empowered to pass legislation that helps them get around the slot controls, and in fact they have done so repeatedly.

Independent aviation journalist Colleen Mondor has written a great two-part series on the history of Congressional “oversight” of DCA operations, which is cited in my bibliography; in order to avoid stepping on toes or retreading the same ground, I wish only to summarize the main points.

The FAA first introduced slot controls at DCA in 1966, along with a so-called “perimeter rule” that restricted flights to 500 miles (800 km) or less. These limitations had become necessary because the number of passengers had already begun to exceed the capacity of the airport terminal facilities, and because the number of aircraft was disproportionate to the number of gates available, resulting in delays after landing. The slot controls were intended to solve the gate capacity problem, while the perimeter rule was intended to encourage larger airplanes operating longer flights with more passengers to land at Dulles instead, leaving DCA for regional flights that carried fewer passengers, reducing the strain on terminal-side infrastructure. However, this had the side effect of prohibiting direct flights to the home constituencies of many congressmembers, who were so incensed that they accused the FAA of relegating people from more distant regions to the status of “second-class citizens.”[14]

Ever since these limitations were first introduced, members of Congress have used their votes on critical legislation as bargaining chips to secure exemptions from the slot controls, the perimeter rule, and various proposed caps on passenger turnover. Consequently, by the mid-1980s the perimeter had been relaxed to 1,000 miles (1,600 km) and several statutory carve-outs existed to permit even longer routes to certain cities.[14]

In 1987, the Department of Transportation successfully secured legislation transferring control of Dulles and National to the locally-governed Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority, which some thought would end direct federal control over DCA operations. However, the bill that created the MWAA included provisions ensuring continued “congressional oversight” of the authority; expanding the perimeter to 1,250 miles (2,000 km); and limiting the number of air carrier slots to 37 per hour, down from 40, with a clause stating that the number could not thereafter be changed except for safety reasons, effectively precluding any further increases.[14]

Congress soon found that this rule could be circumvented by inserting language into the FAA’s periodic funding reauthorization bills establishing certain “exemptions” to the 1987 law. These exemptions were usually added in order to secure votes from members of important legislative committees. For example, in 1997, Arizona Senator John McCain, then chair of the Senate Commerce Committee, threatened to hold up a billion-dollar MWAA renovation project unless 24 more slot exemptions were granted to DCA, including flights to the west coast; he eventually got his wish, and the flights were added into the FAA reauthorization bill in 2000[20], along with a provision that struck the prohibition against the FAA changing the number of air carrier slots.[64] Then in 2003, congressmembers from Illinois and Alaska lobbied for more, and got their wish again; followed by even more in 2012, now at the behest of Senators from Oregon and Washington, despite the protests of the MWAA, who told Congress that they had no vacant gates, no vacant ticket counters, and no additional parking. And in 2023, the same fight came up again, as an industry group backed by Delta Air Lines proposed adding even more slot exemptions; congressmembers who stood to benefit from the new flights backed the proposal over the protests of the FAA, and the exemptions were successfully inserted into the 2024 FAA reauthorization bill.[20]

In order to understand how the addition of ever more slot exemptions has affected operations at DCA, I spent several days reading federal statutes and examining excel spreadsheets containing data on slot allocations, traffic counts, and airline timetables. What follows is my analysis of the resulting operational dynamics. This part is kind of dull and boring, but once you understand it, you start to see why operations at DCA became so badly strained, and ultimately how that strain laid the foundation for the disaster that followed. I promise that this will all be very enlightening.

◊◊◊

A slot exemption, in the most basic sense, is a slot that is awarded in addition to the slots baked into 14 CFR Part 93. These exemptions are listed in the US Code under 49 USC 41718 “Special Rules for Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport,” where paragraph (a) awards 24 daily slot exemptions; paragraph (b) awards 20, paragraph (g) awards 16, and paragraph (i) awards 10, for a total of 70.[15] The MWAA website states that there are 64, so I’m not entirely sure whether I’m reading the law incorrectly or if the MWAA’s numbers are outdated, but either way, it’s one of those two numbers.[16]

The way these slot exemptions work is that the airlines to which they are awarded may use them in any of the slot-controlled hours, from 06:00 in the morning to midnight, provided that no single hour contains more than 67 slots.[1:77][17] Therefore, while the Code of Federal Regulations lists 60 hourly slots for DCA, a number that can only be changed by the FAA for safety purposes, Congress has effectively left the FAA powerless to control the actual maximum number of flights into DCA unless it finds that the current traffic levels are unsafe.

Now, for the purposes of further analysis, I went to exclude the 12 slots that are awarded to general aviation and air taxi traffic, because most of these slots are not used. Therefore, in terms of scheduled passenger flights, the FAA limit is 48 per hour, with Congress’s slot exemptions allowing up to 7 more, for a maximum of 55 in any given hour.

According to the FAA Slot Office’s tables of slot awards for the winter 2024–2025 season, applicable at the time of the accident, every window except 6:00, 22:00, and 23:00 hours had more than the 48 air carrier slots envisioned by 14 CFR Part 93, with most hours from 8:00 to 21:00 having either 52 or 53 slots, peaking at the maximum of 55 slots for the 16:00 hour. The total number of slots awarded beyond the regulatory 48, according to the table, was 67; I wasn’t able to determine why this number matched neither the MWAA count of 64 nor the total of 70 from the U.S. Code.[18]

It also has to be explained that a slot is either a takeoff or a landing, not both. The number of landings, which is of primary importance for this story, is always much less than 55, but is also subject to something called an arrival rate.

The arrival rate is an ideal value set by the FAA based on the expected airport capacity, as determined by a comprehensive analysis of various factors, including but not limited to the number of runways, their relative configurations, the type of traffic, the approach aids available, the air traffic control facilities, and so on. The airport is not supposed to receive more arrivals per hour than this ceiling value, although air traffic control can authorize additional landings if necessary.

At DCA, there are two traffic flow configurations, called “north” and “south” respectively. In the north configuration, aircraft land and take off on runways 1 and 33; in south configuration, they use the reciprocal runways 19 and 15. Which configuration is used depends on which way the wind is blowing, because airplanes like to land and take off into the wind. In the north configuration, some small aircraft can also take off on runway 4; runway 22 is never used due to airspace restrictions.[4–8:48:30]

At the time of the accident, the maximum arrival rate in the north configuration was 36 per hour in visual meteorological conditions (VMC); 34 in marginal VMC; 32 in instrument meteorological conditions (IMC — that is, clouds); and 30 in low IMC (i.e., fog).[1:74] In other words, when the weather was clear and the north configuration was active, the airport was expected to be able to accept landing traffic at a rate of up to one landing every 100 seconds. A 2014 FAA analysis of actual air traffic movements at DCA appears to be the origin of this number, as it shows that the maximum achieved traffic turnover in any one-hour window during the study period was 36 takeoffs and 36 landings in the north configuration.[19]

You might notice that 36 takeoffs and 36 landings amounts to 72 traffic movements, five more than the maximum of 67 slots per hour. You might also recall that the 12 general aviation and air taxi slots are partly unused, meaning that this figure of 72 probably consisted disproportionately of airliners, resulting in an even larger exceedance of the airliner slot limit of 55. This raises two points that we need to address: first, the use of this fact as justification for adding more slots; and second, the reason why this turnover rate was observable despite the existence of the slot system.

Regarding the first point, legislators and officials cite data like these to justify their additions every time Congress adds more slot exemptions. For example, during the 2003 expansion, a Department of Transportation spokesperson insisted that DCA could “comfortably handle” the expansion; similarly, in 2024, the lobbying group Capital Access Alliance argued that the data supported the addition of 40 to 50 new slots, although in the end they won only ten.[20] Studies like the one I cited above add fuel to these arguments because they appear to show that not all of the available runway capacity is being used. On the other hand, the MWAA and FAA correctly pointed out prior to these expansions that gate availability was already a problem and would only get worse if more flights were added, regardless of what the runway capacity was.[20] The need to wait for gates to open up would cause further flight delays at an airport that was already infamous for them. In fact, a 2023 FAA memo to the Office of Government and Industry Affairs stated that “The [Capital Access Alliance] report’s analysis claiming to show that DCA can support the increase is flawed and does not directly tie to the physical airport capacity.” The memo went on to argue that DCA already had the 5th highest number of ground delay programs and ground stops in the country, and that adding 25 daily flights would increase delays by a further 33%.[21]

The second point I wanted to make is that slot allocations don’t automatically translate into real-world aircraft movements, because real life is messy and imperfect. While researching for this article, I used DCA traffic count data from the week leading up to the accident to analyze how many airline flights took off and landed during each hour, what runways they used, and how those numbers compared to the slot allocations and arrival rates — and what I found was that the level of correspondence was wildly variable. For example, on 23 January 2025 — a randomly selected day from that week — I found that while 95% of the awarded slots were indeed used, the actual number of aircraft movements during each slot-controlled hour varied from as high as 10 above the number of allocated slots to as few as 21 below.[22] This is because US airline schedules are not Japanese train schedules; they’re really more of a general suggestion of when the plane might depart or arrive. In fact, using the MWAA’s departures and arrivals board for DCA, I observed aircraft movements during peak hours on a randomly selected day, revealing that a substantial portion of arrivals and departures scheduled within any given hour actually took place in a different hour, sometimes because they were late, but more often because they were early.[23]

This is likely because airlines increasingly use block schedules, meaning that the scheduled arrival time is the outermost limit of a 20- or 30-minute range during which the arrival is expected to occur, allowing airlines to count more on-time flights as early, and more delayed flights as on-time. The schedules themselves showed evidence of this practice in the form of scheduled arrival times clustered at the very end of the hour. For instance, during the day I spent observing traffic, 18.5% of all flights arriving in the 19:00 hour were scheduled to arrive in the last two minutes of the hour; and the 20:00 hour was even worse, with nearly 25% of arrivals scheduled to land at exactly 20:59.[23] This was probably because the slot allocation for those flights was within the 20:00 hour, so the block schedule couldn’t be extended beyond 20:59 without forfeiting the slot. In reality almost none of these flights arrived near the scheduled time; most arrived considerably earlier.

Additionally, controllers have complained that airlines deliberately stretch the slot rules by packing flights disproportionately into the last 30 minutes of an hour and the first 30 minutes of the next, allowing them to schedule more flights per rolling hour than the slot rule permits, without violating the cap of 55 per calendar hour. This creates “periods of compacted demand” that strain the airspace and runway capacity without necessarily being reflected in the benchmarks used to measure short-term traffic volume. LaGuardia combats this tactic by limiting both the number of slots available in each 30-minute period, as well as the number that may be used in any two consecutive 30-minute periods; however, DCA has no such rule.[1:280]

The lesson here is that while no more than 55 slots may be allocated to a given hour, the inherent randomness of airline schedules can and sometimes does push the actual number of airliner movements significantly above the allocation. For example, during the 10:00 hour on 23 January 2025, there were 62 airliner movements; the following day, during the 16:00 hour, there were 61.[22] NTSB investigators stated during their public hearings on the accident that hours with as many as 70 or more movements were also observed,[4–3:19:00] corroborating the 2014 FAA study’s maximum observation of 72, and if we include “rolling” 60-minute periods overlapping two calendar hours, air traffic specialists from the DCA area stated in interviews that numbers as high as 80 had been recorded.[24:546] Obviously these exceedances were a regular occurrence, and when asked at the hearings whether this was a concern for air traffic control, the DCA Manager for Air Traffic Control Operations, Clark Allen, testified that it was.[4–3:19:00]

It has nevertheless been argued that because the twelve general aviation and air taxi slots are seldom used, leeway exists for these kinds of exceedances, because the additional airliner movements simply eat into the unused capacity originally awarded to air taxis. But again, the reality is not so simple.

In 1991, around 175,000 air carrier movements occurred at DCA, a number that had increased to 294,000 by 2024. At the same time, the number of air taxi operations fell from 118,000 in 2007 to only 1,600 in 2024, and general aviation movements fell from more than 32,000 in 2001 to less than 3,000 in the years after the 9/11 attacks. By these metrics, the number of total aircraft movements at DCA has actually fallen over the last 25 years.[1:56] But not all traffic is created equal. Most of the air taxis and general aviation flights were small aircraft capable of using runways 15/33 and 4/22, leaving the primary runway 1/19 for the airliners. Replacing 145,000 small aircraft with 119,000 additional airliners caused the two shorter runways to fall into relative disuse, while most of the new air carrier traffic had to be jammed onto runway 1/19 because it was the only runway long enough to reliably accommodate those aircraft types.[1:56] As a result, by the 2020s on average 93% of all arrivals in the north configuration were landing on runway 1, while only 7% used runway 33.[1:201] Therefore, the replacement of a large number of general aviation and air taxi operations with a smaller number of air carrier operations actually increased the strain on DCA’s main runway, and by 2023 runway 1/19 had become the busiest single runway in the entire United States, with an average of 819 daily aircraft movements.[1:90]

The conclusion that has to be drawn here is that the underutilization of the 12 hourly general aviation and air taxi slots is not indicative of unused airport capacity as far as air carrier operations are concerned, because replacing small aircraft movements with air carrier movements decreases traffic on the already underutilized runways and increases it on the runway that’s already busy. Therefore, the near-daily exceedances of the theoretical airliner slot limit of 55 per hour are a cause for concern not only in terms of gate and terminal capacity, but potentially runway capacity as well. And in order to analyze whether this is in fact the case, we need to dive into the theoretical versus actual arrival rates at DCA.

As I mentioned earlier, the clear-weather maximum arrival rate at DCA in the north configuration, active at the time of the accident, was 36 aircraft per hour. For the south configuration, this number was slightly lower, at 32, due to certain airspace constraints. Now, it has to be noted that arrival rates considerably higher than this can be achieved, and indeed were achieved during the 2014 FAA study I cited earlier, but only at the expense of departure rates. In fact, the highest arrival rate recorded in that study was 45, but this occurred during an hour with relatively few departures.[19] This is because arrivals and departures alike mostly use runway 1/19, meaning that departures have to be slotted in between arrivals to the same runway. If the arrivals are too frequent, there won’t be enough time for a departing aircraft to taxi onto the runway, accelerate, and become airborne during the window between when the previous arrival vacates the runway and the next arrival touches down. Air traffic control rules prohibit issuing clearances that would result in two aircraft being wheels-down on the same runway at the same time, for obvious reasons.

Therefore, the maximum arrival rate of 36 per hour assumes an equilibrium of arrivals and departures. If all of those 36 arriving aircraft land on runway 1 — they don’t, but let’s pretend for a moment that they do — then you would have 100 seconds between each arrival to get a departure out, resulting in the figure of 36 arrivals and 36 departures that was the optimum experimentally observed balance during the 2014 FAA study. In order for this to work, everything has to go absolutely perfectly — if even one aircraft is cleared onto the runway before it’s ready and takes 20 seconds to finish a checklist, or if even one aircraft is too slow to vacate the runway after landing, then the frenetic equilibrium will be thrown off and the 36/36 arrival/departure rate won’t be achieved. And because no human system is perfect, running for an entire hour without either of those things happening is incredibly rare. Again, though, this analysis doesn’t account for aircraft diverted to runway 33, which I’ll come back to in a moment.

In order to understand the arrival rates that are actually achieved on a day-to-day basis at DCA, I went back to the traffic count data from the week before the accident and checked how many arrivals occurred during selected peak hours. My goal was just to get a sense of how often DCA was operating near its maximum arrival rate. What I found was that the maximum was reached nearly every day, especially in the south configuration. For example, on January 23, the south configuration arrival rate of 32/hour was reached during the 18:00 hour and exceeded during the 16:00 hour, when 34 aircraft landed, presumably at the expense of some scheduled departures. On January 24, the north configuration was in effect, and during the 16:00 hour there were 35 arrivals, only one below the maximum. On the 26th, the 15:00 and 18:00 hours hit 34 arrivals each and the 20:00 hour hit 35; and on the 27th, the south configuration maximum was matched during the 20:00 hour and exceeded in the 13:00 and 16:00 hours — and so on and so forth, you get the idea.[22]

The use of runway 15/33 is crucial to achieving these numbers. The traffic count suggests that during arrival-heavy hours in the north configuration, around 5 arrivals use runway 33 instead of runway 1, leaving an effective maximum arrival rate of about 31 for runway 1.[22] The advantage of diverting some arrivals to runway 33 is that the next departure can be cleared for takeoff as soon as the aircraft landing on 33 clears the intersection with runway 1, whereas if the arrival had been on runway 1, controllers would have to withhold takeoff clearance until the arrival had taxied off the runway entirely.[4–2:51:20] Therefore, if one landing is on runway 33, a departure can be slotted in between two arrivals that are closer together than would otherwise be possible.

If all these numbers seem tight to you, you wouldn’t be alone. In fact, even if we account for aircraft normally offloaded to runway 33, the effective arrival rate of 31 per hour for runway 1 is still much higher than at other airports with similar runway configurations. At San Diego International Airport, one of the busiest single-runway airports in the country, the FAA has set the maximum arrival rate on its primary runway at just 24. At Long Beach, which similarly has a busy main runway with a shorter, less-utilized crossing runway, the maximum arrival rate is also 24; and at Palm Beach, which has a nearly identical configuration to Long Beach, the maximum arrival rate is either 26 or 28 depending on the direction of flow. All of these numbers are well below the arrival rates prescribed for DCA.[1:76] So why is DCA’s maximum arrival rate set so high? Is the process really being applied equitably to all airports, or is DCA being treated differently?

There is in fact plenty of evidence that controllers considered DCA’s arrival rate to be too high. A controller I spoke with who works at a different slot-controlled facility said that any time the actual number of arrivals gets within five of the maximum, their job gets quite difficult, so one can only imagine having to deal with that kind of traffic for multiple hours every single day. More to the point, in 2023 the Potomac TRACON, which feeds aircraft from high level airspace into the DCA approach capture area, drafted a memo requesting a reduction in the arrival rate. The request was filed because airlines were increasingly using larger aircraft in order to maximize their passengers-per-gate ratio, meaning that the percentage of aircraft small enough to land on runway 15/33 was decreasing. The corresponding increase in traffic on runway 1/19 was making it difficult for the TRACON to space aircraft far enough apart for the tower to squeeze takeoffs in between them.[1:73–74] Remember what I said about those arrival intervals and what happens if the pilots and controllers don’t get the timing perfect on every takeoff and landing? That’s right, you either delay a bunch of departures, or you delay a bunch of arrivals, and you get told by your boss to “make it work.” It’s a no-win scenario.

In light of these facts, the Potomac TRACON calculated that the maximum arrival rates for all configurations and weather conditions should be reduced by four across the board, using numbers derived from the FAA’s own guidance for setting arrival rates. According to the sworn testimony of Potomac TRACON Air Traffic Manager Bryan Lehman, he drafted a memo requesting the lower arrival rates and submitted it to the district manager for review prior to formal escalation.[4–3:06:20] Ten days later, the district manager informed the TRACON that they would not address the arrival rate issue because the FAA funding reauthorization bill was up for a vote at the time,[4–3:08:00] and instructed them to “stand down the memo” because it was “too political.”[24:824]

The implication was that with Congress seeking to expand the number of slot exemptions, any action by the FAA to reduce arrival rates into DCA would be seen as undermining the will of those legislators backing the expansion, causing them to withdraw their support from the funding bill unless the FAA reversed course. The math bears this out. During an hour awarded the maximum of 55 airliner slots, achieving an equal number of arrivals and departures would require an arrival rate of 28; and the original arrival rates were all equal to or greater than this number except in conditions of low IMC in the south configuration, which was very rare. But if the arrival rates were reduced by four across the board, now the maximum arrival rate would be below 28 in the south configuration anytime conditions were less than completely clear, greatly increasing the number of days where airlines could not use all of the slots awarded by Congress. This effect would also spill over into peak afternoon hours where airlines relied on the high arrival rates to land 34 or 35 aircraft per hour, forcing the airlines to delay or cancel some of those flights even when the weather was clear. And that would mean Senator Maria Cantwell’s flight from Seattle and Senator Ted Cruz’s flight from Houston might be cancelled more often. What a catastrophe!

To be clear, this pressure didn’t come from Congress alone. In his NTSB interview, which was not under oath, Lehman also said it was an open secret among DC-area air traffic personnel that American Airlines had “a lot of pull” when it came to ATC practices and scheduling issues.[24:545–546] American Airlines, its regional subsidiary PSA, and its contractor Republic Airways collectively hold approximately two thirds of all air carrier and commuter slots at DCA[18] and consequently has considerable lobbying power in Congress. Therefore, the local procedures, policies, and, yes, arrival rates may be influenced as much by the needs of American Airlines as the needs of capitol hill. But in my opinion the buck stops with the legislature that writes the laws.

In the end, although the TRACON’s request for lower arrival rates was smothered in the cradle, the Traffic Management Officer for the FAA’s Washington District, Njuen Mandi Chendi, testified that she nevertheless attempted to reduce some of the strain on runway 1/19 by performing outreach to airlines in order to increase utilization of runway 15/33. According to her testimony, prior to 2023 most airline pilots would decline requests to use those auxiliary runways because they didn’t have landing performance numbers ready; but as a result of her outreach, airlines began encouraging pilots to calculate their runway 15/33 landing performance in advance, ultimately increasing utilization of that runway.[4–3:10:00] This would have had the side effect of putting more aircraft into conflict with helicopters, as we will see in part 3, without solving the underlying problem. However, the data shows that after 2023, the percentage of aircraft landing on runway 33 actually continued to fall,[1:201] thus the strain does not appear to have been relieved by her efforts.

Everything I have laid out so far points to the conclusion that the amount of airliner traffic at DCA during peak hours was excessive. Controllers requested lower arrival rates; the existing arrival rates were higher than those at similar airports; and the FAA’s own process for determining arrival rates produced a lower number. Furthermore, arguments suggesting that the reduction in air taxi and general aviation traffic has created unused capacity are misleading; and while traffic levels may be comfortably below the FAA’s stated runway capacity most of the time, spikes that approach or even exceed the limits occur nearly every day. And all of this is to say nothing of gate and terminal capacity, metrics that proponents of increased operations often ignore in favor of runway capacity (although these ground-side issues are not relevant to the accident).

Despite these facts, there remains a subset of the aviation community that is deeply skeptical of the notion that there’s anything wrong with DCA traffic levels. For example, a February 2025 article by View From the Wing argued against a post-accident reduction in the arrival rate because “the FAA has estimated capacity when the 3 runways are in operation at significantly greater than what’s been used in recent years,” and suggested that the only people who think DCA is overcrowded are “NIMBYs” and “United Airlines.” (And I suppose the air traffic controllers who complained about the arrival rates are just crybabies who should suck it up?) Regardless, the article appears to be written without a correct understanding of what the original arrival rate actually was or what it would take to replace unused air taxi slots with air carrier slots.[25] That doesn’t stop politicians from pointing to such surface-level analysis to argue that adding more flights is perfectly fine.

One of the primary mistakes made by the View From the Wing article was to assume that because the actual arrival rates during most hours don’t approach the maximum, the difference must represent unused capacity.[25] This is only true in Barbie World, where everything is perfect, and every flight is scheduled exactly 100 seconds apart and every plane arrives exactly on time and every takeoff is smoothly slotted in between them, day in and day out, forever. As I’ve already made clear in this Chapter, that’s not how the real world works, and it’s not how airline schedules work. The actual rate of arrivals rises and falls in huge waves like a storm-tossed ocean, receding into easily manageable troughs and periods of flat water before building into monstrous breakers that threaten to overwhelm the tower. The max arrival rate itself is not a magical barrier where everything is fine if the number of scheduled arrivals remains below it, or where chaos instantly takes hold if it’s exceeded. Instead, it’s supposed to be an estimation of the limit required to prevent the inevitable waves from becoming too high, too frequently. Think of it like a bathtub with a wave generator in it, and the arrival rate is the water level. If the arrival rate is set too close to the limit of what is operationally possible — that is, too close to the rim of the tub — then the waves will splash out of it more often.

All evidence indicates that at DCA, the waves were splashing out of the tub on a regular basis because the arrival rates were too high. The NTSB came to the same conclusion, citing an “unsustainable arrival rate” among the contributing factors to the accident.[1:299] How exactly this problem affected air traffic control practices in a way that contributed to the disaster will be discussed in more detail in Chapter 4. But for now, the takeaway from Chapter 2 should be that DCA was and still is under considerable stress due to excessive traffic, and that while the FAA is theoretically responsible for regulating traffic levels, inappropriate pressure from Congress has made the problem worse while simultaneously hamstringing the FAA’s ability to do anything about it. Certainly we should never have to read in an accident report that employees on the ground who tried to improve safety were rebuffed because their request was “too political.”

Chapter 3: Helicopters Amok

Up until now, I’ve focused on fixed-wing aircraft operations at DCA, but these represent only one layer of airspace use. Even as airliners pour in orderly columns toward National Airport, dozens of helicopters crisscross the region, darting this way and that, circling, hovering, taking off and landing at the numerous heliports, hospitals, and military bases that surround DCA on every side. From an airline pilot’s perspective, the helicopter activity in Washington appears random and unpredictable; some at PSA assumed that the helicopters operated in a “wild west” environment with no obvious rules.[26] But in reality, there is a method to the madness.

Anyone who has lived in Washington, D.C. will remark on the frequency with which helicopters are heard overhead, especially compared to other major American cities. Major helicopter operators in the DC area include but are not limited to all four main branches of the US military and the Coast Guard, municipal and county police forces, air ambulance companies, and VIP transport flights. Within 10 kilometers of DCA, airspace charts show nine civilian and military heliports plus eight helicopter pads at medical facilities, for a total of 17 helicopter facilities,[27] which I know to be an undercount because the military helipad at Joint Base Anacostia-Bolling, directly across the river from DCA, is not shown (and therefore others may not be either). In addition, helicopters operating out of more distant locations like Fort Belvoir or Walter Reed National Medical Center, to name but a couple, also regularly transit the airspace around DCA. The traffic count data for the eight days leading up to the accident includes no less than 913 helicopters that transited the DCA tower’s area of responsibility during that week, amounting to 114 per day, with the number of unique helicopters per hour varying from none to as many as a dozen.[22]

Helicopters typically operate at low altitudes under visual flight rules, or VFR, meaning that the pilots navigate visually with respect to landmarks, regardless of whether or not they’re in contact with air traffic control. To assist with VFR navigation of complex airspaces with high traffic density, the FAA publishes nine local helicopter route charts, including one for the Baltimore-Washington region. These charts depict numbered routes for helicopter pilots to follow that can be referenced during communications with air traffic control, as well as a prolific quantity of additional information useful to VFR helicopter pilots, including the locations of landmarks, lighted and unlighted obstacles, restricted areas, geographical features, airports, heliports, highways, airspace boundaries, ATC frequencies, altitude restrictions, radio navigational aids, and so on and so forth.[27]

This chart, and the routes depicted on it, would find themselves at the center of the investigation into the crash of flight 5342. And to truly tell the story of the now-infamous helicopter routes, we need to start with their history — which takes us back to the 24th of September, 1985.

At that time, the Baltimore-Washington VFR Helicopter Route Chart as we know it today did not yet exist. Instead, military helicopters in the DC area navigated the complex airspace over the nation’s capital using their own Special Military Helicopter VFR Route Chart, which was not published for civilian use, although some civilian operators had managed to get their hands on it anyway. Individual military units’ Letters of Agreement (LOAs) with the DCA tower allowed them to request and accept clearances based on routes depicted on the special military chart, but civilian operators’ LOAs did not.[28]

On the 24th of September that year, a controller manning the tower’s helicopter control position — more on that in Chapter 4 — cleared a helicopter for liftoff from DCA’s north helicopter pad, which no longer exists but was at that time located just west of the departure end of runway 1. The helicopter belonged to a civilian operator that had somehow acquired the special military chart, so the pilot requested a departure via “Route 1 to Greenbelt.” I was never able to find a copy of this more than 40-year-old military chart, but if Route 1 was the same as it is today (and the evidence supports that it was), then the route presumably ran from Cabin John, Maryland, southeast down the Potomac River to Hains Point, immediately north of DCA, then northeast up the Anacostia River to Greenbelt, Maryland. Since the DCA north helipad was not located directly under Route 1, a departure via this route would have required what’s called a “transition,” in which the helicopter follows a normal agreed-upon path to, from, or between a published route or routes.[28]

The helicopter controller said that she always told helicopters departing the north helipad for Route 1 to fly northwest to the Arlington Memorial Bridge, where they could intercept the route and follow it to their destination without interfering with traffic taking off or landing on runway 1/19 (then known as runway 18/36). This transition was informal and not published on the special military chart. In this case, when the helicopter pilot asked for Route 1 to Greenbelt, she cleared the helicopter to fly as requested, but incidentally forgot to specify the transition that should be used. As a result, the helicopter pilot assumed he had been cleared to Route 1 by the most direct transition, which took him directly over the departure end of runway 36 (now 1).[28]

At the same time, the Local controller, who was responsible for issuing landing, takeoff, and runway crossing clearances, cleared an Eastern Air Lines Boeing 727 for takeoff on runway 36 without coordinating with the helicopter controller. As the 727 neared its decision speed, the pilots suddenly saw the helicopter take off from the north helipad and fly toward their projected takeoff trajectory. At the last second, the captain aborted the takeoff and slammed on the brakes. Simultaneously, the helicopter pilot saw the 727 approaching and steered hard away from the runway, back toward the helipad. Behind him, the speeding 727 ran off the end of the pavement and lurched to a stop in the grass, just 40 meters from the edge of the Potomac River.[28] By the narrowest of margins, disaster was averted.

The NTSB found that the helicopter operator didn’t have an LOA with the tower authorizing its pilots to request or accept clearances based on the special military chart, but that the controller had no way of quickly ascertaining this. Furthermore, because it wasn’t intended for civilian use, the chart only depicted standard transitions to and from military heliports, excluding civilian helipads like the one at DCA. As a result, the NTSB recommended that the FAA create a single VFR helicopter route chart for use by all helicopters in the DC area, both military and civilian.[28]

Because the special military chart is, as far as I can tell, lost media, I wasn’t able to definitively establish the closeness of the relationship between the pre-1985 military chart and the Baltimore-Washington VFR Helicopter Route Chart that the FAA published in 1986 at the behest of the NTSB. However, I have plenty of reason to believe that the helicopter routes themselves were most likely adapted with few, if any, significant alterations.

One reason why I believe the helicopter routes were either copied directly from the military chart, or were otherwise designed mainly to accommodate the needs of the Department of Defense, is that Route 1, the route to Greenbelt requested by the incident helicopter pilot and the only special military route specifically discussed in the NTSB report on the 1985 incident, still leads to Greenbelt today.[27]

Another reason is that the US military was by far the largest helicopter operator in the DC area at the time and still is today, accounting for 79.2% of all helicopter traffic using helicopter routes within 5 nautical miles of DCA.[1:200] This is largely because civilian and law enforcement operators mostly don’t fly from a fixed point A to a fixed point B. Police and news helicopters tend to circle for long periods in a particular area in order to follow an event on the ground, and medevac helicopters have to fly to wherever the patient happens to be, which is usually nowhere near the handful of published helicopter routes. Military helicopters, on the other hand, are there to fulfill specific missions, requiring them to fly between the same points over and over again.[3–3:08:00] As a result, the FAA added “police zones” to the chart, allowing law enforcement and civilian helicopters to circle inside a particular area with defined boundaries that can keep them separate from helicopters that might be circling in other zones. These zones deliberately avoided overlapping with some of the major helicopter routes, emphasizing the distinct operating models they were designed to accommodate.[27] Therefore, there would have been few stakeholders in the helicopter route design other than the US military.

The identity of the organization that first drew the helicopter routes — and I do believe it was the Department of Defense — is important because it helps explain some of the glaring shortfalls in the route design. But before I discuss those problems, we need to look at what exactly a helicopter route is, in the legal sense.

Each helicopter route is depicted on the chart as a wide blue line that typically follows a visually distinctive route, such as a river or a highway or a chain of specified landmarks. Although the blue lines bear some resemblance to a corridor of airspace, they’re purely illustrative, because the routes don’t actually have defined lateral boundaries. For example, the pre-accident route chart stated that Route 4 should be flown “via the east bank of the Potomac River,” but nowhere did it say how close to the east bank one needed to be, nor was any similar information provided for any other route either.[1:46] The routes did include specified altitudes, although the chart contained contradictory information. An info box labeled “recommended route altitudes” stated that an altitude with a line under it was a minimum, an altitude with a line over it was a maximum, and an altitude with both lines was “recommended,” while a separate info box said “all altitudes are maximum,” leaving it unclear whether any altitudes were recommended or mandatory.[1:45]

FAA personnel testified at the NTSB hearings that the helicopter routes, in and of themselves, carry no regulatory force. Therefore, all minimum and maximum altitudes were in fact “recommended” and the only way to decide whether a helicopter was too far from the route centerline was personal judgment. In the FAA’s view, the purpose of the routes was to provide named paths that could be referenced to facilitate communication between pilots and air traffic control. The idea was that instead of saying “I want to fly to point B via points C, D, E, F, and G,” a pilot could just ask “I want to fly to point B via Route 3,” and the controller would clear as requested, with a mutual understanding of where the helicopter would go.[1:42:43] An unapproved deviation from the route would constitute a violation of an ATC clearance, but not a violation of the route itself, because the routes are non-regulatory and cannot strictly speaking be “violated.”[3–7:02:30]

Several of these helicopter routes passed in close proximity to DCA. Route 1 came within approximately 1 kilometer of the northeast side of the airfield at its closest approach before angling away up the Anacostia River, with a maximum altitude decreasing from 1,300 feet at Cabin John to 200 feet east of the Arlington Memorial Bridge. Route 6 crossed directly overhead the center of the airport from west to east with a recommended altitude of 1,500 feet, well away from any departing or arriving aircraft. And most importantly for this story, Route 4 branched off of Route 1 at Hains Point, located at the confluence of the Anacostia and the Potomac Rivers opposite DCA, and then proceeded south down the east bank of the Potomac past the Woodrow Wilson Bridge, paralleling the runway 1 approach corridor at a maximum altitude of 200 feet. The centerlines of Routes 1 and 4 crossed the approach corridors for runways 19 and 33 at distances of approximately 2.3 and 1.1 kilometers from the runway thresholds, respectively.[1:44]

Incredibly, the proximity to the approach corridors into DCA did not appear to have been considered in the design of the helicopter routes. Although the greatly reduced route altitudes in the areas near the airport gave the impression that the 200 foot maximum was intended to vertically separate helicopters from DCA-bound aircraft, no such separation actually existed. In fact, a helicopter traversing Route 4 along the eastern shore of the Potomac River at the maximum altitude of 200 feet would pass just 75 feet below the optimal 3-degree glide path into runway 33. Away from the shore, this margin further reduces toward zero at a rate proportional to one’s charitableness in interpreting the location of the route’s undefined western boundary.[1:207–208]

FAA personnel explained that the helicopter routes were never intended to provide separation from fixed-wing traffic approaching DCA or any other airport, and for good reason. In order to guarantee separation for a helicopter flying inside the route, it would need to be an instrument flight rules or IFR route, defined with respect to GPS coordinates and navigational aids. But helicopters mostly fly under visual flight rules with respect to landmarks, so an IFR route would be useless to virtually all helicopter operators.[26] The helicopter chart therefore included only VFR routes, but a VFR route that relies on a pilot’s judgment of their distance from landmarks rather than the readings of instruments inherently cannot have strictly enforceable boundaries, which in turn means it is fundamentally incapable of guaranteeing separation from traffic on other routes.

Considering these facts, it remains unclear why exactly the maximum altitude on routes 1 and 4 decreased to 200 feet in the area of National Airport. The low maximum altitude might have been a mitigating measure intended to reduce the likelihood that helicopters would pass directly through the approach and departure corridors for runways 1/19 and 15/33 without technically guaranteeing anything, but if so, it was at best ineffective and at worst actively misleading. The only remotely effective solutions would have been to establish a very high minimum altitude, far above any landing airplanes, or even better, to give DCA a wide berth and avoid establishing helicopter routes so near to the runways in the first place. But remember, the helicopter routes weren’t created by the FAA — they were created by the Department of Defense. And as we will see in Chapter 5, the DoD didn’t care very much about the impact of their mission on civilian air traffic. They wanted a low altitude route down the Potomac River past DCA, so they got one.
